name: Opioid use disorder
summary: Medications for OUD include the full agonist methadone (dispensed for OUD only through certified opioid treatment programs), the partial agonist buprenorphine (sublingual/buccal daily products and weekly or monthly extended-release injections), and the antagonist naltrexone (monthly extended-release injection; oral tablets labeled for opioid blockade). Since the 2023 Consolidated Appropriations Act removed the DATA (X-) waiver, any clinician with a current DEA Schedule III registration may prescribe buprenorphine for OUD; labels advise co-prescribing or recommending an overdose reversal agent.
plainSummary: Opioid use disorder is a medical condition where a person keeps using opioids even though it causes harm. Medicines like methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone lower cravings and withdrawal and greatly reduce the risk of overdose and death.

approved.indication: Detoxification treatment of opioid addiction (heroin or other morphine-like drugs) and maintenance treatment of opioid addiction, in conjunction with appropriate social and medical services. Limitation of use: when used for detoxification or maintenance of opioid addiction, methadone is subject to the conditions for distribution and use in 42 CFR Part 8 and may be dispensed only by certified opioid treatment programs (OTPs).

population.ages: Adults (safety and effectiveness below age 18 not established per label)

dosing.start: 20–30 mg single supervised dose (initial dose not to exceed 30 mg); may give an additional 5–10 mg after 2–4 h if withdrawal persists
dosing.target: Clinical stability most commonly at 80–120 mg/day
dosing.max: First-day total ordinarily ≤40 mg; no fixed maintenance maximum (titrate cautiously because methadone accumulates over the first days)
dosing.notes: Steady state takes 3–5 days; deaths have occurred from cumulative effects during early titration. Use lower starting doses when tolerance is uncertain (e.g., no opioid use for >5 days). Many CYP3A4/2B6/2C19/2C9/2D6 interactions; monitor QTc in patients with risk factors. For OUD, dispensed only by certified OTPs (federal exceptions exist, e.g., hospital treatment of a patient admitted for another condition).

formulations: Dispersible tablets for oral suspension 40 mg
Oral solution 5 mg/5 mL, 10 mg/5 mL
boxedWarnings: Risks from concomitant use with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants
Accidental ingestion (especially children) can be fatal
Misuse, abuse, and diversion of opioids
Interactions with drugs affecting cytochrome P450 isoenzymes
Conditions for distribution and use of methadone products for the treatment of opioid addiction (42 CFR 8.12; certified OTPs only)
contraindications: Acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or without resuscitative equipment
Known or suspected gastrointestinal obstruction, including paralytic ileus
approved.plainSummary: Methadone is a long-acting opioid medicine given once a day at a special clinic to stop withdrawal and cravings. It has to be started slowly and carefully because too much too fast can be dangerous.

verified.note: Indication, boxed warning, contraindications, induction/maintenance dosing, and pediatric statement checked on the Methadose concentrate label (rev. 4/2026). The approval year (1972) is from the history of federal OTP regulation and was not shown on the label. Methadone 5/10 mg tablets also carry pain indications; the Dolophine brand is listed as discontinued in Drugs@FDA.

approved.indication: Treatment of opioid dependence; preferred for induction. Should be used as part of a complete treatment plan that includes counseling and psychosocial support.

population.ages: Adults (safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients not established)

dosing.start: Day 1: 8 mg in divided doses (2–4 mg increments), given once there are objective signs of moderate withdrawal and at least 4 h after last opioid use; Day 2: up to 16 mg once daily
dosing.target: Usually 4–24 mg once daily (16 mg/day is the recommended post-induction dose)
dosing.max: No labeled maximum; label notes doses above 24 mg/day have not been studied in RCTs but may be appropriate for some patients
dosing.notes: Label prefers buprenorphine-naloxone for unsupervised maintenance; mono-product reserved for induction or naloxone intolerance (and commonly used in pregnancy). For patients on methadone or long-acting opioids, mono-product induction is recommended. Moderate–severe hepatic impairment: consider dose adjustment. Taper gradually when stopping. New 4 mg and 12 mg tablet strengths were approved July 2026.

formulations: Sublingual tablets 4 mg, 12 mg (some generics, approved 2026)
approved.rems: Buprenorphine Transmucosal Products for Opioid Dependence (BTOD) REMS
approved.plainSummary: Buprenorphine is a medicine that dissolves under the tongue and calms withdrawal and cravings while making overdose less likely. It is usually started when a person is already feeling some withdrawal.

verified.note: Label effective 7/2026 includes the new 4 mg and 12 mg strengths (FDA approved July 10, 2026, per the FDA overdose-prevention timeline). The label has no boxed warning. Subutex brand is discontinued per Drugs@FDA. REMS name is from the FDA timeline, not re-checked on the REMS site.

approved.indication: Treatment of opioid dependence, as part of a complete treatment plan that includes counseling and psychosocial support.

population.ages: Adults (safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients not established)

dosing.start: Suboxone/generic: Day 1 up to 8 mg/2 mg in divided doses (start 2 mg/0.5 mg or 4 mg/1 mg, titrate every ~2 h); Day 2 up to 16 mg/4 mg once daily. Zubsolv: Day 1 up to 5.7 mg/1.4 mg; Day 2 up to 11.4 mg/2.9 mg
dosing.target: Suboxone/generic: generally 4 mg/1 mg to 24 mg/6 mg once daily; Zubsolv: 2.9 mg/0.71 mg to 17.2 mg/4.2 mg once daily
dosing.max: No labeled maximum; doses above 24 mg/6 mg (Suboxone-equivalent) have not been studied in RCTs but may be appropriate for some patients
dosing.notes: Zubsolv 5.7 mg/1.4 mg gives buprenorphine exposure equal to 8 mg/2 mg Suboxone. Use the sublingual route during induction. For patients dependent on methadone or long-acting opioids, induction with mono-buprenorphine on Days 1–2 is recommended. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment; naloxone exposure rises in moderate impairment. Label states there is no maximum recommended duration of maintenance treatment.

approved.rems: Buprenorphine Transmucosal Products for Opioid Dependence (BTOD) REMS
approved.plainSummary: This medicine combines buprenorphine with naloxone, which helps prevent misuse by injection. It is taken once a day under the tongue or in the cheek to control cravings and withdrawal.

verified.note: Suboxone film (rev. 12/2025) and Zubsolv (https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=5f5cfcfe-d52b-49e6-8fe4-550477332dd2, rev. 12/2025) were both checked. Suboxone tablets, Subutex, and Bunavail are discontinued per Drugs@FDA; generic tablets and films are marketed.

approved.indication: Treatment of moderate to severe opioid use disorder in patients who have initiated treatment with a single dose of a transmucosal buprenorphine product or who are already being treated with buprenorphine; part of a complete treatment plan that includes counseling and psychosocial support.

population.ages: Adults (safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients not established)

dosing.start: 300 mg SC after a single transmucosal buprenorphine dose (e.g., 4 mg) and observation; second 300 mg dose may be given as early as 1 week later
dosing.target: 100 mg SC monthly after two 300 mg initial doses
dosing.max: 300 mg monthly maintenance may be considered when benefits outweigh risks
dosing.notes: Healthcare-provider administration only; SC in abdomen, thigh, buttock, or back of upper arm (alternate sites added Feb 2025). Maintenance injections at least 26 days apart. Monitor after first injection for worsening withdrawal or sedation.

formulations: Prefilled syringe 100 mg/0.5 mL, 300 mg/1.5 mL (subcutaneous)
boxedWarnings: Risk of serious harm or death with intravenous administration (forms a solid mass; occlusion, thromboembolic events)
Available only through the SUBLOCADE REMS (certified healthcare settings and pharmacies)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to buprenorphine or any component of the ATRIGEL delivery system
approved.plainSummary: Sublocade is a monthly buprenorphine shot given under the skin by a clinician, so a person does not need to take a daily dose. It must never be injected into a vein.

verified.note: Label rev. 7/2026 reflects the February 2025 label change: rapid initiation after one transmucosal dose, second dose at 1 week, and alternative injection sites.

approved.indication: Treatment of moderate to severe opioid use disorder in patients who have initiated treatment with a single dose of a transmucosal buprenorphine product or who are already being treated with buprenorphine; part of a complete treatment plan that includes counseling and psychosocial support.

population.ages: Adults (safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients not established)

dosing.start: New to buprenorphine: 4 mg transmucosal test dose, then Brixadi weekly 16 mg; add 8 mg within 3 days (week-1 total 24 mg), with an optional further 8 mg ≥24 h later
dosing.target: Weekly 16–32 mg or monthly 64–128 mg (transmucosal 8–10 mg/day ≈ 16 mg weekly/64 mg monthly; 12–16 mg/day ≈ 24 mg weekly/96 mg monthly; 18–24 mg/day ≈ 32 mg weekly/128 mg monthly)
dosing.notes: Weekly and monthly products are different formulations and cannot be combined. Patients already on transmucosal buprenorphine can switch directly to weekly or monthly. Starting the monthly product in new entrants has not been studied. Dosing window is ±2 days (weekly) or ±1 week (monthly). Needle cap contains latex.

boxedWarnings: Risk of serious harm or death with intravenous administration (forms a liquid crystalline gel; occlusion, thromboembolic events)
Available only through the BRIXADI REMS (certified healthcare settings and pharmacies)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to buprenorphine or any other ingredient
approved.plainSummary: Brixadi is a buprenorphine shot given under the skin once a week or once a month. New patients can start the weekly product after a test dose; the monthly product is for patients already receiving buprenorphine.

approved.indication: Prevention of relapse to opioid dependence, following opioid detoxification; part of a comprehensive management program that includes psychosocial support.

population.ages: Adults (safety and efficacy in pediatric patients not established)

dosing.start: 380 mg deep IM gluteal injection after an opioid-free period of at least 7–10 days
dosing.target: 380 mg every 4 weeks (once monthly), alternating buttocks
dosing.notes: Oral naltrexone lead-in is not required. Confirm absence of physiologic dependence (consider naloxone challenge). Patients switching from buprenorphine or methadone may be vulnerable to precipitated withdrawal for up to 2 weeks. Loss of tolerance raises overdose risk after missed doses or discontinuation; offer an overdose reversal agent.

formulations: 380 mg vial of microspheres + diluent kit for intramuscular injection
contraindications: Failed naloxone challenge or positive urine opioid screen
Hypersensitivity to naltrexone, PLG, carboxymethylcellulose, or diluent components
approved.plainSummary: Extended-release naltrexone is a monthly shot that blocks the effects of opioids, so using them does not produce a high. A person must be fully off opioids for about 1–2 weeks before the first shot.

source.label: DailyMed: VIVITROL (naltrexone for extended-release injectable suspension)

verified.note: First generic approved July 2023 (FDA timeline); an Amneal generic naltrexone kit is listed on DailyMed.

approved.indication: Blockade of the effects of exogenously administered opioids. Not shown to provide any therapeutic benefit except as part of an appropriate plan of management for the addictions.

population.ages: Adults (safe use below age 18 not established)

dosing.start: 25 mg once; if no withdrawal signs, 50 mg/day thereafter (after an opioid-free interval of at least 7–10 days for short-acting opioids)
dosing.max: Alternative supervised schedules: 100 mg every other day, 150 mg every third day, or 50 mg weekdays + 100 mg Saturday (label notes possibly higher hepatocellular injury risk with single doses >50 mg)
dosing.notes: Consider a naloxone challenge if occult dependence is suspected. Effectiveness depends on adherence; the label stresses measures to ensure the patient takes the medication. Overdose risk is higher after stopping because tolerance is lost.

contraindications: Current opioid dependence, including maintenance on methadone or buprenorphine
Failed naloxone challenge or positive urine opioid screen
approved.plainSummary: Naltrexone pills block the effects of opioids so they do not produce a high. They work only if taken regularly, and a person must be off opioids before starting.

source.label: DailyMed: Naltrexone hydrochloride tablets USP 50 mg (SpecGx)

verified.note: The label wording is 'blockade of the effects of exogenously administered opioids', not 'opioid use disorder'. ReVia brand is discontinued per Drugs@FDA. The hepatotoxicity boxed warning is no longer present on the current generic label.
